steps.text: Explore the Serra do Caramulo in central Portugal, where the July 2026 wildfire began near Tourelhe.

layers.caption: This satellite image shows the hills and valleys of the Serra do Caramulo before the wildfire.

steps.text: Move the slider to see how two satellites show the same landscape.

layers.caption: This image uses reflected sunlight to show the landscape in natural colour.
In this radar image, brighter areas sent a stronger echo back to the satellite.

steps.text: The wildfire was reported near Tourelhe, in Vouzela, at 03:04 local time on 2 July 2026.

layers.caption: The Tourelhe marker locates the reported ignition area.

steps.text: The next day a Copernicus satellite photographed the smoke from the fire near Vouzela, drifting out over the Atlantic Ocean.

figure.alt: Satellite image of north-west Portugal. A long plume of grey smoke rises near Vouzela and stretches west across the Atlantic Ocean.
figure.caption: Copernicus Sentinel-3, 3 July 2026, 10:38 UTC. At that moment the plume was about 620 km long.
figure.credit: © European Union, 2026, Copernicus Sentinel-3 imagery (EC – DG DEFIS)

steps.text: On 4 July the national civil protection commander said the fire was spreading at an average of 765 metres an hour, about 600 hectares an hour.

layers.caption: The marker shows Tourelhe, the name given to the fire. Lusa placed the ignition there; the ICNF report lists Chamusqueiros as the place where it started.

steps.text: On the morning of 3 July the fire was reported out of control on the slope of the Serra do Caramulo. A local fire commander told Lusa that Matadegas had been evacuated overnight and Mançores was being evacuated, and that resources were few, with some villages having none. Reports differ: on 4 July Lusa wrote that vulnerable residents of both villages had been taken from their homes, and the mayor of Tondela said no village was evacuated.

layers.caption: The map locates the two communities named in the reports.

steps.text: On 4 July the flames reached Daires, in the Caramulo area, and kept burning with intensity near several villages. The mayor of Tondela said Daires was not evacuated, and that she had received no reports of injured people or destroyed property in the municipality.

layers.caption: Daires is the village the fire reached on 4 July.

steps.text: The fire was reported under control at 12:40 local time on 5 July 2026.

layers.caption: The map shows communities and landmarks associated with the fire.

steps.text: The wildfire burned through the Cambarinho Botanical Reserve.

layers.caption: The reserve marker is located at the start of the Cambarinho walking trail.

steps.text: Compare the dashed area, inside the burned zone, with the ground around it. Coherence tells how much the radar signal changed between two passes of the satellite: low coherence means it changed a lot. Between 29 June and 11 July, the passes before and after the fire, the signal inside the dashed box stopped matching, so the colour is strongest there and fainter outside.

layers.caption: Orange marks low coherence: the signal over the ground changed between the two passes.

steps.text: Compare the radar measurements across the fire with those from the following 12 days.

layers.caption: Radar echoes were less similar between the two passes across a broad area on the northwestern slopes of the Serra do Caramulo, stretching from Tourelhe towards Águeda.
In the two passes after the fire, radar echoes were more similar across much of the same area.

steps.text: Use the official ICNF perimeter to see where the low-coherence pattern overlaps the mapped burned area.

layers.caption: This image shows where radar echoes were less similar between the passes on 29 June and 11 July.
The outline marks the area that Portugal’s forest agency, ICNF, mapped as burned.

steps.text: Radar brightness depends on the surface. Calm water acts like a mirror: it sends the radar beam away from the satellite, so a reservoir sends back almost nothing and shows as the darkest area. The Ribeiradio reservoir, on the Vouga river, sits at the dark end of the scale.

layers.caption: Dark means a weak echo, as over this water. Bright means a strong echo, as over rough ground.

steps.text: Compare two radar channels from the same overpass and look for areas that appear bright in one channel and dark in the other.

layers.caption: In this HH image, the radar sent and received waves in the same orientation.
In this HV image, the radar received echoes turned sideways, which can happen when waves scatter through branches and leaves.

steps.text: Radar brightness measures the strength of a return from one pass, while coherence measures how similar the radar signals were across two passes.

layers.caption: One possible reason some burned areas still appear bright is that standing trunks may continue to reflect radar waves.
Lower coherence shows where radar echoes were less alike between the two passes, which can indicate a change on the ground.

steps.text: Compare the 11 July and 16 August HV images and look inside the burned area: on average it gets slightly darker over the summer, while the land around it hardly changes.

layers.caption: The 11 July HV image shows the radar return shortly after the fire.
The 16 August HV image shows the radar return over the same landscape later in the summer.

steps.text: Compare the pair that spans the fire with a pair from October. Both cover 12 days. In October the burned area no longer shows low coherence, which means little changed between those two passes, not that the land has recovered.

layers.caption: This pair spans the fire: the signal changed across the burned area between 29 June and 11 July.
In October, three months after the fire, both passes are after the fire and the burned area no longer shows low coherence.

steps.text: Tondela's town council began working with a University of Aveiro researcher on a package of measures to reduce the effects of the fire on the slope of the Serra do Caramulo.

layers.caption: The ICNF perimeter gives a geographic reference for discussing post-fire recovery.

steps.text: Explore the available dates and layers, then follow the official perimeter to see where the radar pattern changes.

layers.caption: This coherence map provides a starting point for exploring the changes observed across the fire.
The ICNF outline helps you compare the radar signal inside and outside the mapped burned area.
